utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic, of Ms. Nikolic, of Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. Haynes. Prosecution, I see Mr. McCloskey, Ms. Soljan, Mr. Mitchell. All right. Let's start from here. We were advised that you probably wouldn't be here today, Mr. Nikolic, due to the unfortunate passing away of your father. It's a sad event, which unfortunately every one of us has to pass through. I passed through that several years ago. I know what it means. And therefore, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to convey to you our deepest sympathies and our condolences not only to you but to the rest of your family. Our heart is with you on such an occasion. THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to thank you for expressing your sympathies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if at any time during the sitting you wish to leave us, please do so at any time. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Judges. On behalf of my client, and he has just expressed it himself, the expression of sympathy of the Trial Chamber are very much appreciated. My colleague had the opportunity to visit Drago Nikolic at the UNDU this morning and he has expressed both the will and the intention to be here this afternoon, but as the Trial Chamber has suggested, we will assess as the day progresses and I will see him at the break and see what his condition is at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this brings another related issue I would like to inform the Trial Chamber of at this time is of course with such an incident, it was initially our intention to immediately file for a motion for provisional release of Drago Nikolic in order to attend the funeral. However, we will not be doing so because after discussing the matter with Mr. Nikolic, and of course in accordance with the Serbian tradition, the memorial services has to take place 40 days after the passing away, and we will be filing such a motion in the coming days once we have all the information and of course bearing in mind that we will be suggesting to the Trial Chamber that be he be provisionally released with the strictest of conditions so that he can pay the last respects to his father 40 days after the passing away. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We met this morning as we usually do, as you can imagine we meet regularly outside court hours to discuss the several issues relating to the trial, and we met this morning to take stock of the situation as it obtains at present, and it seems to us that the way we are going, we would finish with the Defence case for accused Popovic towards or at the end of the coming week, and that's a conservative estimate which basically means that at the same time, either towards or at the end of next week, the next Defence case will need to start, and that's why I'm looking at you now, Mr. Ostojic. I also know that very rightly so, you have shown interest in this already and are preparing actually to be able to start your case. Without in any way diminishing the principle that the management of the case is yours and yours alone, and we rather take the stance of doing our best not to interfere; at the same time expecting the optimum from each Defence lawyer as equally as from the Prosecution, we thought of making some suggestions which would help organise the proceedings the best possible, and that would be in your own interest and in the general interest because we have a responsibility to manage the case. I think you need to keep these days that I have mentioned in mind and prepare accordingly, but running parallel to that, I think there is a responsibility which I am sure you have already been thinking about of at least indicating to the Prosecution the names of the first group of witnesses that you intend to bring forward. I'm even informed that you've been working on this, so what I am saying may be somewhat redundant but please try to attend to do that. Secondly, we are drafting our decision on your motion relating to 92 bis and 92 ter witnesses, and pending and in anticipation of that decision which we will hand down soon, we are formally and orally informing you to take it for granted that those 92 bis witnesses which are mentioned in paragraph 1 of the Prosecution's response of the 9th of June, and to whom the Prosecution has not objected, are going to be admitted as Rule 92 bis witnesses. That is without cross-examination. Which leave us with perhaps the most crucial issue, and believe me, out of not only a sense of duty but also the respect that we have for each and every one of you, we tried to understand as much as we could the conclusions or the import of your last filing, but somehow we feel that we can't see clear as to who is being renounced to and who isn't, what is the exact position. So we thought of trying to solve this in the simplest way possible, namely that now that you know that a certain number of 92 bis witnesses are going to be admitted as such, and more or less you can read and understand your last filing better than we can from our point of view, we would like you to file, by Monday, an updated 65 ter list of witnesses that you intend to bring over. In the meantime, you would have provided the Prosecution with a list of the first group of witnesses. Do you wish to comment, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. My comment is we have actually provided to the Prosecution that first group of witnesses I think a week or two ago, by e-mail. We are working with the witness and protection unit to coordinate passports, visas. There are some problems that we didn't anticipate such as the speed of the trial thus far but I think we will be able to produce that first group and I think we've identified 12 witnesses and we hope to call out of those 12 if everything goes well, eight in the first week and we also plan, as I think I've indicated, at least orally to the Prosecutor, that we are going to have the second week, the week of our experts, which will be four. And I think in closer examination of our 65 ter list, without getting into too much detail, we have withdrawn several witnesses based on some of the suggestions made by the Court and our re-review of it. We have also identified and we will be filing, as the Court instructed, by Monday, some of them are joint witnesses so they really don't even fall within the time frame that we requested but we did add that time just for a matter of convenience, there is approximately seven what we've called joint witnesses that several other accused have adopted or we've adopted their witnesses, so the list is getting pared down. I think it's going to reasonably, if the Court would like me to estimate, we think will take approximately, from my best guesstimate in scheduling it, approximately six weeks, no more than that. I think we are going to call approximately 35 or 40 witnesses in total. Again it depends on some of the objections raised by the Prosecution. There are I think four that are in dispute where they would like to at least bring them in for both direct and cross-examination. I think we stated our position on that. I don't think the Prosecution without going into the merits here now, have reasonably raised that issue but that's where we stand on it. I will be filing that as the Court instructed by Monday and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, thank you so much. That's very good to hear. Basically as I said, our only problem is that reading through all the material, it wasn't quite clear in our mind where we stand. So now I think it's already clearer and by Monday, I think it should be crystallised.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise if it wasn't clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- but we will certainly make it as clear as possible by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, that happens and we would have dealt with you differently if we saw a shortcoming, which we didn't see. So thank you. We left yesterday with the documents that needed to be tendered. Ms. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon, everybody in the courtroom. Yes, we have attached our list and we would like to add to that that one document, 1D1196 should be under seal. 1D1196. This is on the first page of our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections from the other co-accused? No? There are no translation issues here, no? I leave it to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: From what we can see from our exhibit list Exhibit 1D1139 still has an outstanding translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, translation requested. Okay. So all these will be admitted with the caveat that where there is no translation as yet, that will be marked for identification in the interim period until it is translated. Okay. Next witness -- do you have any -- sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we would like to tender into evidence two documents. One is document P03471, which was shown to the witness yesterday. And the other document we would like to offer into evidence is the script that Mr. Kovacevic was reading from yesterday that we obtained from him during the break and the 65 ter for that would be P03478.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We object to the admission of this document because it is not relevant for the witness's testimony at all. He was not reading from that document while testifying. He just consulted his notes every now and then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To you wish to comment, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I would very briefly. We do believe that these notes, the script indeed, is relevant and probative for the validity, for checking the quality, the substance and the credibility of this witness's testimony. As an expert witness, we don't believe that he should be referring to prompts or already pre-ready made answers as he in fact was doing during the course of the testimony yesterday. I do agree that there was one set of notes, figures, that were purely figures and we are not asking for that to be admitted into evidence. However, I can indicate at least one example in evidence where there was -- from the script of about 13 pages there were questions and then there would be an answer typed out in italics which in effect was read word for word or verbatim by this witness. In our opinion, if this is -- if the -- the Trial Chamber should see that these were pre-prepared answers because the basic question is whether these are the views of an objective expert or whether these are pre-prepared views that were prompted by the Defence, and this is I think especially important in light of the comment that the witness made in the course of his testimony yesterday where he said that his primary goal here was not to derive or prove that a certain list is good or not but to try to bring into dispute the list produced by Brunborg and Urdal, so we would ask Your Honours to consider that and take into account that there were pre-prepared answers or at least prompt of answers that somebody who is an expert should really not be referring to, especially when they are referring to the ways in which his report was prepared, prompts about dates of underlying source documents he was referring to, et cetera. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic, and that will be the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday, we did suggest that the notes should be read out before the Trial Chamber because we believe that there was no reason for these notes not to be presented to everybody in the courtroom. The task of this witness in the case was to assess Helge Brunborg's work and his findings. This is exactly what he did. In his notes, there are reflections on what he read out in Brunborg's findings. Again, I am kindly requesting you to allow us to read out all that in front of everybody, if you're agreeable to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tapuskovic. Let's hear what Madam Fauveau has to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you make a determination on that point, Your Honour, I would like to say that as far as the Miletic Defence were concerned, we were not aware of the contents of these notes. These notes were given to the Prosecutor and not to the Defence. Therefore if the Prosecutor intended to tender this document into evidence, these notes should have been disclosed to the other Defence teams yesterday or this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Brief observation. Following on from that, I'm bound to say I perhaps wasn't following yesterday's cross-examination as closely as I should have done, but the rather bold assertion made by my learned friend Ms. Soljan, was it put to the witness? Because otherwise in our submission it's worthless unless the witness has had a chance to deal with that fairly serious allegation that she has just made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There were some questions yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There were direct questions as precisely to the fact that there were already written answers to certain questions, yes. That was put to the witness yesterday and he answered it, yes. I need to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that some of these notes were put to the witness yesterday and questions asked, but also bearing in mind what both you, Madam Fauveau, and you, Madam Tapuskovic, have raised equally, considered to be valid points, we are of course admitting the page that you have indicated but we are also admitting it to form a part of all of the whole. In other words, what we want in the records are all the notes and not just that page. Okay? That would make it easier for us to consider weight and also cover or make good for the shortcoming that Madam Fauveau raised very rightly, in fact. And also the point made by -- all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's entirely clear and in fact when I said I was going to be offering the script, I meant the entire 13 pages, not just the one example from page 4 that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we must have misunderstood you. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you would give me the 65 ter number again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think it has. I don't think it has because this was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be in by the end of the day as P03478.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the Prosecution please tell us what documents that they take over from witness Kovacevic when they spoke to him yesterday? We don't have that list and we would kindly ask them to provide us with photocopies of what they are tendering into evidence. We would like to know which papers did they select among those that Mr. Kovacevic had on him during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can show you the two documents that we have from him. One is the 13-page list or script as I was referring to and which we have asked to get admitted into evidence. The other one is a one-pager that has numbers, figures, and we have no objections to that nor do we intend to offer that into evidence. Those were the only ones but you were -- in fact the counsel for the Defence was present when we took over those notes, so they should have been aware, and the registry took those and photocopied them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, we would like to have the photocopies of that in order to see what is being tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That can be arranged. Mr. Zivanovic, if you wish to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. First we would like to know what documents they take from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what she said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What documents they selected to tender to the evidence, it is very important for us what was criteria for selecting documents they asked to tender right now. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't understand the last point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They took some documents from the witness. I don't know what number of documents they took, what number of pages they took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but that has been explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what selection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That has been explained by Ms. Soljan already. She told you that there were two types of documents. One is this document consisting of notes contained in 13 pages, and the other one a page containing some figures, which they don't intend to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they took more than two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am being -- we are being informed actually that the papers were collected from the witness, not by the Prosecution but by the registrar, and that the papers collected were those that have been indicated by Ms. Soljan and not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know they took all documents from him, all documents he had in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we are being told and that should suffice. Yes, Mr. McCloskey? I see you standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was just going to say this was a registry matter following your order and she is exactly correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we weren't here when the whole process was taking place so we weren't in a position to know exactly what happened. But that's it. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to raise an issue related to the fact that these notes have just been admitted into evidence and I just wonder whether this case is an isolated case where the notes are being tendered into evidence because the Prosecution has allegations that he was referring to them or is it a matter that they are notes prepared by an expert witness? I would not like to see that this would be a precedent whereby all notes produced by an expert witness appearing before this Chamber would then become disclosable material. It is very likely that an expert witness before testifying will produce for himself a skeleton that he may or may not refer to, and I don't see why this should become compellable material. I would just like to seek the Court's guidance on this issue, Mr. President, so we can best prepare for the upcoming expert witnesses. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think each case will depend on its own merits and we'll deal with each case if and when it arises and we can leave it at that for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have slightly revised our decision after consultation. There is that other page that Ms. Soljan said was not meant to be tendered. However, since the argument turned on basically also the point as to what documents were obtained from the witness and that page was also obtained from the witness and refers to numbers which, as you may -- I'm sure you would have gathered is fundamental for the witness's testimony, we would like that document to be included with the other batch, that page to be included with the other batch, and they will form together one exhibit, all right? Which will be given a 65 ter number or an exhibit number later on and they of course need to be translated because they are in the witness's original language which we don't understand. Thank you. Can we bring in the next witness, please? Now, this witness is common to or a joint witness for four Defence teams, that's you Mr. Zivanovic, you Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Nikolic -- Mr. Bourgon, and Mr. Gosnell. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, depending on the examination-in-chief that will be conducted by my colleague, we do not intend to ask any questions and we rely upon his examination-in-chief in order to save time for the Court. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the same, I think, for the time being is indicated by the Borovcanin Defence team for which I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You've been summoned as an expert witness by no less than four of the accused. That's namely accused Popovic, Beara, Nikolic and Borovcanin. Before you start giving evidence, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be speaking the truth in the course of your testimony. Please read out the solemn declaration aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Zivanovic, who will introduce himself, soon will be the first to go. He will then be followed by others on -- with several questions, and we will do our utmost to finish with your testimony the earliest possible. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor Dunjic. Although we know each other, I will still introduce myself. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and I represent Vujadin Popovic in this case. First of all, I would kindly ask you to tell me your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: My name is Dusan Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1950 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something about your educational and professional background?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I am a professor of forensic pathology at the school of medicine in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about your educational background and what about your specialist training that you've done in the past?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I specialised in forensic medicine. Before that, I obtained my master's degree and after that I got my Ph.D., all of which were in forensic medicine and all that from the school of medicine in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about your professional background? What jobs have you held and where?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Our primary task is to work at university, which means we educate medical students, and my particular subject, forensic medicine, is part of year five at the school of medicine in Belgrade. And within my teaching activities as a professor, I also appear as a forensic pathologist before all the courts in my country and in the surrounding countries as well as here at the Tribunal. As far as my experience is concerned, I apologise, I can say that I do about 200 post-mortems a year independently or with my younger assistants and that I have had 100 to 200 forensic opinions provided to various courts about all sorts of lethal outcomes, violent or non-violent. In addition to that, I have been engaged as a special expert within the field of forensic medicine in such case -- in the cases such as Ovcara and Vukovar, and there I just observed the work of others. I believe the gentleman's name was Mr. Haglund. I was also engaged by the special court, the Special Prosecutor in Belgrade, in the case of the murder of our Prime Minister, Zoran Djindjic and I was also engaged by the Special Prosecutor in the cases of the so-called Zemun clan and that is as far as my work for the special court is concerned. However, as an expert or a member of expert teams I was also involved in various research for providing my expert opinion as required by the Yugoslav institute for the study of war crimes. I wouldn't be able to give you the exact title of that institute but it is in Belgrade. And for that institution, I was engaged together with my team to examine the detainees who had been released from the camps in Bosnia and Croatia. This was between 1996 and 1998. In 1998, I was a member of the team of the forensic institute in Belgrade which was engaged in exhumations and post-mortems of the victims that had been excavated by the Lake Radonjic for the purposes of the Haradinaj case that was heard before this Tribunal, and on that case I appeared as a witness on behalf of the Prosecution. In addition to that, I have -- I was also engaged between December 2000 and December 2003 while I was director of the institute for forensic medicine, and as such I was engaged by the district court in Belgrade to participate in exhumations, identifications and repatriations of the victims that were found in Batajnica. I also testified about that before this Tribunal in the Milutinovic case, if I'm not mistaken, and Milutinovic and others, I believe. In professional terms, so far I have published a number of professional papers, over 180 of them or even more than that in various publications and magazines both in Serbia and abroad. I have authored a number of books, and one of them appeared only recently. I authored that with a group of authors. I have also authored a textbook which has had three editions, and this textbook concerns the post-mortem of bodies and this is the official textbook of the school of medicine in Belgrade and as such, is used by all the medical students. I would also like to single out another book that I co-authored with a colleague of mine, and this concerns the suicides among adolescents. As far as I know, this is the only medical textbook that has been translated from Serbian into Russian by the Russian academy of arts and sciences. I'm a member of various institutions, at the school of medicines, I am a member of the committee on forensic medicine, I'm also a lecturer and professor at the school of the European centre for peace and development -- of the university for peace of the United Nations. And as far as my work for the Tribunal is concerned here in The Hague, this started in 1999. I prepared an expert opinion in the case of Dusko Tadic, IT 91-1 of the Foca group, IT 96-23. I also provided an expert opinion of the wounds of Zoran Vukovic in the same case, IT 96-23/1. I came to examine Milan Simic on two occasions. I was also engaged on the part of the Defence team in the Galic case, IT-98-29. I was also engaged in the Plavsic Krajisnik case, IT -00-39 and 40 by the Defence teams of the accused. I have been engaged by the Defence of Vujadin Popovic in this case and I also appeared as an expert in IT-04-84-1, as I've already told you. As an expert witness, I have also been heard by the Prosecutor of the Tribunal in the Racak case, because together with my colleagues from Yugoslavia, as it was known at the time, Russia and Finland, I was engaged at Racak to work on the cases of deaths that happened during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just correct a minor error that concerns a name. You said that you were Prosecution expert witness in the case Haradinaj, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, IT-04-84/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Five Defence teams have asked for you to testify here so could you please tell us and the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait a moment, Mr. Zivanovic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I must have missed one, then, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I must have missed one. I have only got four.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five Defence teams were concerned when we requested that Mr. Dunjic testify. All the five accused who have been accused of genocide requested that this witness testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's Pandurevic is included then?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, do you confirm that? Because to my knowledge, there are only four teams that have summoned him as a joint expert witness. Yes, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We summoned the witness, we participated in the agreements with the witness, and when he started drafting his report -- he isn't on our 65 ter list, so in fact he is here for the four Defence teams, although we participated in agreeing on his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you please tell me what the subject of your expert report was to be? What did the Defence want to you do, in fact? What did the Defence teams want you to testify about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I was asked by Mr. Ostojic, Peter Haynes, Aleksandar Nikolic and yourself to do the following. In fact, you assigned me a task. You referred to the documents you had been provided with and you asked me to analyse these documents, the documents, some of which I have brought here with me, although I have others, but I couldn't bring them all, well, the documents on the whole concerned reports from locations examined in the year 2000, 2001 and 2002. Subsequently, I received certain other reports, two CDs in English and the Serbian language. There were various records. Then I was provided with another three CDs. I was given a certain period of time to carry out an analysis and I analysed these collective reports with regard to certain locations and they concerned particular years and certain pathologists, the chief pathologist had already dealt with these cases. Having examined those documents, I understood that in the collective reports, there were quite a few items that I as an expert in forensic medicine had to check up on. In fact, I also had to perform an analysis, and an analysis can be carried out only on the basis of individual reports. Only on the basis of autopsy reports. Or records of autopsies, in fact. So I received a number of these CDs, with these records on them, with these autopsy reports on them, and the last report that I was provided with was on the 19th of April of this year, and if I'm not mistaken, there were 8 DVDs and CDs, 8 DVDs with autopsies performed up until the year 2008. Naturally, given the time I was allocated to perform my analysis I could only select a certain number of cases and a certain number of locations for more detailed analysis and then I could compare these individual reports with the collective ones. Last year I came here too and last year I insisted on a list of all the autopsy reports together with the numbers of the autopsies, linked to the various locations concerned. On the 22nd of February 2007, I was provided with a document that you were given, you forwarded this document to me, that contained a list of 30 locations, and there were 3.281 autopsy reports listed or records.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify something. You said that there were collective reports you were provided with. Could you just tell me something about the professional background of the experts who drafted these reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would just like to confirm what document it was that the witness just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic or Mr. Dunjic straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, would you please provide the Prosecution with the document for his examination?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The date of the document is the 22nd -- it was signed by Peter McCloskey, senior -- this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to end your examination-in-chief there, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I must proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me something about the professional background of the individuals who provided those collective reports? Could you tell me about their professions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll answer that question in the following way. There are collective reports drafted by the chief pathologists, by Mr. Clark, for example, and then there were reports drafted by the investigator Dean Manning, if I'm not mistaken. I think he's an investigator. I mistakenly put the title "doctor" here. And then there were collective reports drafted by an anthropologist who had been engaged to work at a certain location. Then there were collective reports of other investigators who worked at those locations. William Haglund, an anthropologist, for example. And these are reports that I managed to have a look at. And given the different way of describing the problem dealt with, and given the fact that there were various opinions that were expressed as a result of analysing the locations, well, given all of that, I thought that given the number of corpses discovered, it was necessary to carry out a detailed analysis for each location analysed and it was necessary to do this by consulting individual autopsies in order to obtain a valid analysis of the collective reports and the individual reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you've been discussing these collective reports, are these collective reports that were drafted by experts from the Tribunal or rather than by Prosecution experts?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I assume that that is the case. I even listened to Mr. Clark when he testified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying this because you mentioned material that you were subsequently provided with in April 2008. If you can remember this, can you tell us which analysis is concerned and who carried it out, the same experts or others?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I had a look at those eight DVDs and at the end of my analysis, I was very precise. One of the DVDs, there are eight of them, one of the DVDs, the first one, for example, has ten folders and each folder contains a number of files. And a huge quantity of photographs. When I was preparing for this testimony, I printed out one case or rather one file, and it consists of 22 pages. It's the smallest file. And here you can see that this file concerns autopsies that were performed in, let's say, Potocari, exhumation on the 25th of April 2006. And it was not possible for me to analyse any of these documents. I could only prepare it physically, or rather bring it here so that I can show it to you and tell you how many autopsies it concerned. This was done under the supervision of the cantonal prosecution of the Tuzla canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you about. In fact --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I do apologise but as far as these eight DVDs are concerned, well, I would need additional time to analyse all of this to become familiar with the number of cases concerned but the forensic medical aspect is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that given the time allocated to you and given the voluminous material, you weren't able to examine all the autopsy reports. I would now like you to tell me the following: How did you select the material that you examined, the material that, in fact, became part of your report or rather the material that was analysed in your report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: First I analysed the document I was first provided with. It related to Nova Kasaba and there was even a full translation of the autopsy report, so that was a primary grave site, then. I thought it was necessary to examine the characteristics of a secondary grave site. Zeleni Jadar. And then I took Pilica as a primary site and a sample from Pilica and a sample from Ravnice where corpses were found on the surface. So the forensic part that I was interested in consisted of comparing the autopsy findings and of analysing the changes to the corpses at such various locations, because there was a possibility of the corpses having various injuries. So during this time period I tried to perform such an analysis to see what the situation was at the primary site, at the secondary site, to see what sort of injuries had been noted and to see what the situation was with the bodies in Ravnice, in 2000 and 2001, because the bodies were on the surface, and I tried to see what the description of the changes to the bodies was like and to see whether it was consistent with the changes to corpses at other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the locations of Nova Kasaba, Zeleni Jadar, Ravnice. Could you be more specific? Is it one grave site, are there several grave sites? Let's start with Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, Nova Kasaba has, well, there is Nova Kasaba 1, 2 and 3. This is how they have been designated, Nova Kasaba 1, Nova Kasaba 2, and Nova Kasaba 3. But in these reports, there is Nova Kasaba 4. I have to point this out. And in the documents that I had, there is a Nova Kasaba 4 and this only concerns one case. But later on when I had a look at some other final reports, I saw that in Nova Kasaba 4, later when other exhumations were performed I noticed that there were another 19 cases there. I haven't even had a look at those 19 cases. I couldn't find them. And there is Nova Kasaba 6, 7 and 8, and there are a certain number of cases at these sites. I have referred to the cases that I could analyse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we are now dealing with Nova Kasaba, does this mean that you analysed autopsy reports from Nova Kasaba 1, 2 and 3, 6, 7 and 8, but not 4, apart from one corpse, one case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, one case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the other grave site is concerned, the Zeleni Jadar site, could you tell me something about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In this report -- just a minute. Well, there is Zeleni Jadar 5 and there is Zeleni Jadar -- just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can the witness tell us what he's referring to again, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dunjic, can you be more specific as to what you're referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, can you see the pages that are concerned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you immediately. Nova Kasaba 1 -- do you need the ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, just the page.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Page 42. In the English version, 114. 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's an autopsy report or rather -- yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: These are the autopsy reports I have referred to and the documents appear later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let the witness do this on his own. What Mr. Mitchell wanted to know is which document you were drawing from when you started giving your answer a few minutes ago, Mr. Dunjic. Which document were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the transcript of Nova Kasaba 1 autopsy reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We are interested in the other document that the witness has in front of him, just what that other document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would propose that the Prosecution see all documents the witness has in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't see the need for going through all these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can be my guest, sure.

utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, was the witness referring to that document before or not? Was the witness referring to that document when he was answering the previous question or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.text: I don't understand. I was referring to the documents that I analysed and based on those I prepared my report, my expert report. Here you have it. This is my expert report and there is a description of what is being analysed on each page and in that report, I quoted all the analysed things, and the document from which I took everything is this document, which means that I am using the documents that you yourself submitted to me. This is Mr. Harmon's report about Nova Kasaba. There is also a report of Mr. Haglund or whatever his name is, okay. And then Jose Pablo Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would just like to confirm that it's the witness's report in front of him. That's all we are asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is it.

utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Dunjic. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to Zeleni Jadar 5, there are some quoted reports with ERN numbers, and that's a document here. From Ravnice there is also -- there are also quoted autopsy reports. We shall see that through individual analysis. And there is also an analysis of the location -- I apologise -- Pilica. Again, there are documents that I used in preparing my report and in my written report that you have been provided with, for each location I wrote the ERN number under which the autopsy report has been recorded, and I quoted parts of the autopsy report in order to allow you to follow what I'm saying, in order for you to follow my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Mr. Dunjic, as far as I can see, on pages starting with 42, you dealt with Nova Kasaba, and this goes from page 42 and if you can just bear with me --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: 1, 2, 3 and then 4, that's one case. And then Nova Kasaba, 6, 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then it goes from 42 to 72 in B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to tell me this: You reviewed the autopsy reports. Did you review all of them from this location or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: For Nova Kasaba, I reviewed everything that I said, the whole of Nova Kasaba 1, 2, 3, and one case at Nova Kasaba 4, and I also reviewed everything at Nova Kasaba 6, 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What would be your general impression, when you looked at the autopsy reports from all of these locations, can you tell us from your professional point of view, whether there are any -- or rather, whether these reports were done according to the rules of the medical profession or forensic profession?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about autopsy reports and about their form?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Then we are talking about a very standard formula or, rather, a standard form that contains a general part, the findings themselves, and a conclusion. The procedure that is carried out and that has been described in Mr. Clark's report describing the procedure that was applied at all those locations, and Mr. Clark wrote this in his report for the localities Kozluk, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje and Glogova, ERN 00912281-305, the autopsy report, in factual terms, there is a description of all the procedures that the autopsy teams carried out at various locations. The first procedure was the transport of the bodies from the grave to the morgue, the work at the morgue, the post-mortem analysis, the autopsy report or the report on all the autopsies performed. The description of the methodology as was used to perform the exhumation, the post-mortem and so on and so forth is something that I absolutely agree with. This is exactly what our profession accepts all over the world, and I don't have any objection to what was done and how it was done. However, when I started to analyse, and I'm now looking at Nova Kasaba, when I started to analyse the post-mortem report I could see that its form represents the standard form. It has its heading describing the clothes, the personal belongings and everything else and then there is the external examination, the internal examination, dentist examination, the traumatology findings, the evidence found, the cause of death and the way how the person died. This is a very, very standard form, and I have no objections whatsoever to the form of this report. However, when you go into the report, and when you read what it contains, and also when you see what the recommendation or the standard is according to what Mr. Clark said, we will see that there is a huge disproportion there. Namely when it comes to the description of particular things and situations that were found around and on the body, you can see that there is just a very short list of the things, if there were any, but my major objection, and professional omission on the part of the examiner, is the absence of a detailed description of all the observed changes on the corpse, in the body and in arriving at certain conclusions. If you want me to provide you some details and provide a further explanation, I can do that. Let me put it this way: The standard for post-mortems requires that is everything that a pathologist observes should be described in very great detail and this is something that Mr. Clark confirms. Let me just try and find his statements and I'll quote from it. Mr. Clark in his report ERN number 0300 5065 when speaking about the transportation of the bodies from the grave to the morgue, and when he talks about the way work is done in the morgue, says amongst other things the following: "Once the body is taken out of the fridge, the body is entered into several form, then the body is examined fluoroscopically, the post-mortem analysis would consist of the following things as needed," and he lists those things. Taken further removing the clothes, removing the personal belongings, recording relevant findings, the examination of the body including the findings of its integrity, the state of preservation, identifying physical properties, and any natural diseases. In this following paragraph he says a detailed description of wounds both those ante-mortem as well as those that occurred post-mortem. He himself wrote this and he stated that all the procedures were applied and followed. A similar description of these procedures can be found in all the reports of the chief pathologists who authored the final report, the compiled report, and there is no objection there but let me now go to something else. I would like to show you this. The external examination of the bodies, Nova Kasaba 1, body number 1, marked by number 1, that is to say. The clothes are described, as well as the personal belongings which are practically non-existent. There is no ID papers. The external examination of the body reveals the following: Situation, this is a question mark, and you have to say what situation you found. It says complete. I suppose that he's talking about a completely preserved body. Articulation, partial. This is absolutely an insufficient description of the situation or the status of the joints. The only thing that was given is an indication that the articulation is partial. What does this mean? What does this mean to me as an expert? This is just a statement that I cannot analyse, and why is it important? It is important because one knows that if there is putrefaction and decomposition of the soft tissue that were -- wherever the muscle mass is less thick around joints, it will decompose slowly, and where it is thicker, it will decompose not as fast. When we analyse the articulation of the joints, we can also estimate the time of death and the conditions under which the body was found, which in this particular case, not only in this one but in all such cases, this is very important. And now I'm comparing this actually I should be able to compare this to the following statement: The degree of preservation, putrefaction, partial skeletonisation, obviously for a lay person this doesn't mean a thing. This is just a statement of facts. However, for an expert in pathology, this is very important. When he says putrefaction, I know there are several stages in the process of putrefaction until the complete putrefaction of the soft tissues, also known as skeletonisation. Again a question is raised what difference does it make? And it makes a big difference because from the degree of putrefaction to the degree of skeletonisation, there should be a certain time that has to lapse. Several factors influence the putrefaction process, the environment, the manner of death, the wounds, where it was -- am I speaking too fast?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, you're not speaking too fast. So far the interpreters have not had any problems.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would kindly ask the witness to slow down in order to avoid future problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely it's not your day, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Dunjic, please do slow down. The interpreters were obviously very patient and didn't want to interrupt you but you are speeding up a little bit too much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall repeat. From the stage of putrefaction, changes are based on the stage of putrefaction, we can estimate the time of death. That's number 1. What external factors contributed to the fact that some parts of the body putrefy faster and the others putrefy slower? The first thing that's important here is this: What was the situation of the body before it was buried? And whether the putrefaction changes that were stated occurred exclusively in the grave from which the body was excavated. In order to be able to answer these questions, I should have some feedback that has to be recorded in any post-mortem report. And that's why I'm insisting and that's why I'm saying that this description, and I've only taken the first example, this description is absolutely insufficient and incomplete. It doesn't allow me to answer your question, sir. Let's move on and let's look at something else. Internal examination. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we please have question and answer? There was one question a long time ago and the witness went some way -- I think the original question was about the form of the autopsy report and we went quite some way from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which part of the transcript are you referring to? Please. Because one characteristic of this witness is that his answers sometimes take two or three pages. Are you referring to page 28 line 23?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Dunjic. Now I'm going to ask you to tell me this: Since you have told us what should an autopsy report contain, and you started giving us some examples of all this, I would now kindly ask you to tell me this: What parts of the findings should be contained within an autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: An autopsy report should contain the following findings. I apologise. An autopsy report should contain everything noticed in the general part that concerns the external examination, the internal examination, everything that concerns the trauma findings, and finally one should arrive at a conclusion on the cause of death. When I say that this is what is necessary, it means that one has to have a detailed description of what is, in fact, observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So this means that an autopsy finding has to contain three findings, internal, external and the traumatological findings with the descriptions you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We now are discussing Nova Kasaba. So tell me, in general terms, whether these descriptions and the findings that relate to Nova Kasaba 1, 2, 3 and 4, have these descriptions been compiled in accordance with the rules of forensic medicine? And if so -- well, can you tell us in which cases the rules have been respected and which cases they haven't been respected?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I will answer that question, but, Your Honours, first allow me to fully answer the previous question which concerns the internal autopsy report findings and traumatological findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that case I'll put that question to you, since I have to put precise questions to you in order to obtain precise answers. With regard to the internal findings, did you notice any deficiencies when it comes to the autopsy findings from Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In the internal findings, the case of Nova Kasaba 1, 2 and 3, well, the descriptions of the state of bodies observed are quite inadequate. I'm referring to the descriptions of changes in the putrefaction to the corpses that can be observed. This is important for the following reasons. Changes in the putrefaction of corpses, in the corpses, compared with the putrefaction changes to the external part of the corpses and one then describes the organs that exist and the organs that no longer exist because of putrefaction. So such findings have to be it noted in order to assess the time of death and the conditions the body was in up until the time of the autopsy. This is a rule. And then you just come to your conclusions. The second mistake or inconsistency with regard to what Mr. Clark said is -- concerns the detailed description of the trauma report. In the trauma report, in the vast majority of the cases concerned, it is stated that the diagnosis is complete. One says gunshot wound to the head. And in the findings, I cannot check this conclusion, or, rather, this diagnosis because it's not a finding, it's a diagnosis. In order to check this, I would have to have a detailed description. So this is why there is inconsistency here, why there are deficiencies, and finally, as part of this autopsy report, once all of this has been analysed, one arrives at a conclusion that concerns the cause of death, and this has to be noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's time for the break, Mr. Zivanovic, and Mr. Dunjic. We will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dunjic, I wanted to clarify something first. It has to do with an answer of yours at page 21 of the transcript. You mentioned a document, a letter of the 22nd of February 2007 signed by Mr. Peter McCloskey. However, in the transcript, it was recorded as an answer. Could we please put that on the ELMO and clarify it for the Chamber? I don't know whether you are able to understand it because it's in English but could you please tell us what it's about? Is that the document that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is sufficiently legible. You can move the document up and down. My question is this: Did you receive this together with the material we handed over to you in February 2007 when you were here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It happened when I was here in February last year, on the last day, just before I departed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We left off while you were providing explanations for the autopsy reports for Nova Kasaba 1, 2 and 3, as well as the single case from the Nova Kasaba 4 file. My question is this: Can you single out any of the findings that would meet the criteria of forensic medicine and for which you could say were compiled fully in accordance with the principles of the profession?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I carried out a brief analysis of the files, focusing myself on the visual and internal examination. There are inconsistencies in both approaches and descriptions. In a certain way, there are also inconsistencies in terms of what had been agreed upon or what should have accompanied the trauma findings, i.e. there were no detailed descriptions of the injuries. I can mention a few examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please do so that we could identify them.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The first one, NKS 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is P624. It is Exhibit P624, in B/C/S page 145. In English, 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that's in your report. I'm talking about e-court.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, let me have a look. It's 621. I apologise. You wanted to see the first example. In the English it is 120. In the B/C/S 145.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please go to page 2 immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us do that, please. It is page 146. Go to page 146 in the B/C/S and 121 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will read out the trauma finding that we can see here and I will offer my interpretation. Item 1, "Gunshot wound on the right third rib proximally and distally, which corresponds to the holes in the clothes. Item 2, gunshot wound on the left side, question mark, pelvis, at the place of -- at the place at which the sacrum and iliac bone join. The direction is practically vertically down. Item 3, wrists tied on the back." That is the trauma finding. Why does it not meet the standard requirements? First of all, it does not correspond according to any or all of the criteria of the profession of forensic medicine. It also does not correspond to what Mr. Clark mentions in his summary, in his collective report, as per the methodology. He stated there that detailed descriptions of wounds were offered. However, we do not see that here. Your Honours, when one says gunshot wound and then continues, it's an assertion stating that that injury was killed by a bullet from a firearm. That's a diagnosis. In order for the diagnosis to be of any value for the Court or anyone else for that matter, it must have come out of the trauma finding, which needs to be detailed. That means that we have to have a description of the wound and a description of the injury. It needs to contain all of the elements, size, edges, canals, remaining tissues, any other substances in the canal itself, the exit point, et cetera, et cetera. Once a person writes all that down, a forensic expert, and we will have an opportunity to see good descriptions, in that case, anyone in my profession would be able to conclude that it was a gunshot wound. If not, such as in this case, one needs to choose whether to believe it or not and that is the insufficiency of this trauma finding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, are we looking at the correct English page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It doesn't seem to correspond. Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I think it's page 125, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's check.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, that's correct page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In how many cases, when discussing Nova Kasaba 1, 2, 3 and the single finding in file 4, did you come across incomplete or inappropriate findings from the point of view of forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: When analysing, and I've been through the Nova Kasaba files on several occasions, I saw that in most of the descriptions of the internal and trauma findings we only have the diagnoses and that there are some descriptions of the internal findings which are partially correct. If you're asking me about a particular example which would be a correct one, then I can cite the example in which we have a more precise description, and it is the very next example, NKS 1-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is page 129 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the number of the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S, it is 148. In the English 120 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's it. The next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let us have a look at page 149.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an example of a good description of the trauma changes that have been noted. In item 1 of the finding it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I don't know whether we have the English page. 130. It should be 130. Professor, please do continue.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I will read out the trauma finding. In item 1 it says gunshot wound, the radius of which is 1 by 1 centimetre in the temporal occipital region, and internal cone-like damage on the left side of the skull, partially reaching the left part of the back of the head, as well as the left temple and the area of the maxilla. Item 2, sequential fractures on the right collar bone and the second right rib, from the back towards the front side, without clear cone-like damage that would correspond to a gunshot wound. 3, fracture of the left ribs, T-7 and T-8, as possible exit points of the fractures mentioned in item 2. What did I want to say about this example? In item 1 of the trauma finding we have a relatively precise description of the damage caused by the bullet, no discussion about that. Any forensic medical professional could clearly interpret that. In items 2 and 3, the person who carried out the autopsy did not notice the clear cone-like damage which would be characteristic of a passage of a projectile, and he or she described it as such. In item 3, the person mentioned the fracture of the ribs T 7 and T 8 as the possible exit wounds of the fractures mentioned in item 2. Neither on the ribs nor the thorax there are no clear indications that is these injuries were caused by a bullet. There is the trauma, however, but there were -- there was no indication that that is indeed what had happened. I have to say about this trauma finding that it had been drafted correctly, and from which one can conclude that this person sustained one gunshot wound in the back of the skull. This is not in dispute and is completely acceptable from the point of forensic medicine. However, the other two traumas described on the other parts of the body cannot be ascribed to any gunshot wounds. What follows from such a finding is a wrong conclusion on the cause of death. In the cause of death, which is two paragraphs below, we have multiple gunshot wounds. However, in the findings, we have only one gunshot wound which had been established beyond dispute. So that is the inconsistency between what the person doing the autopsy saw and the conclusion on the cause of death. If I may, I really do have to offer a comment on the cause of death. Not only in this case but generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was to be my next question, the cause of death. I don't know whether you have any comments to offer concerning the autopsy findings you studied concerning Nova Kasaba 1, 2, 3 and the single case of Nova Kasaba 4.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In all the cases referred to from Nova Kasaba, the cause of death has been established. However, and I'll repeat this, well, first I have to deal with the theoretical part of the matter. The cause of death represents a certain situation, either a wound or something else that results in death, if there is a wound to the head, if the head is injured in any way or if there is some sort of a fatal illness that leads to death, well, then this is the cause of death. But for a wound, for a trauma of any kind, I'm not only referring to gunshot wounds, for a trauma of any kind to be a cause of death, it's first necessary for the person to be alive before dying, in other words. The wounds must have provoked certain reactions in the individual concerned. A corpse is a medical fact. Damage to the skull as a result of being hit by a projectile is a medical fact. But for that medical fact to have meaning for a Tribunal, it is necessary for this to be demonstrable and it must be possible to check up on such claims. For such a wound that is described as a wound to be considered as a cause of death, an autopsy has to have a detailed description stating that the wound was inflicted while the individual was still alive. If there is no such evidence, and there is no such evidence when we have putrefied corpses because these corpses have no soft tissue, well in such cases there are only facts that have to be assessed on the basis of other evidence collected by the Court and not by forensic expert. So it's my job as a forensic expert to note that there had been changes as a result of putrefaction and then to say, for example, that the corpse has changed because of putrefaction. That's one of the items contained in the conclusion. Another item would be to mention quite specifically what the findings were, when the autopsy was performed on putrefied body I should state that I noticed that there was a gunshot wound. Item 3, for example, if there are any other wounds or fractures, one should say that there were fractures to the rib cage and so on and so forth that could have been a result or were a result of injuries inflicted by a blunt instrument, and that would be it. If I'm dealing with a putrefied body, I cannot observe any wounds that would show that the individual was wounded when still alive. In other words, for something to be a cause of death it is necessary for this wound to have been inflicted when the individual was still alive. If a gunshot wound caused death, you need to demonstrate that the wound was inflicted while the individual was still alive. And this is how one can provide the Court with adequate evidence and approach the matter in a professional way. That's all. On the basis of a fairly good description, one arrived at a certain conclusion, and I know why, because a number of documents have been compiled about this in the report, stating how it was established that cause of death should be described, certain wounds should be taken to have been inflicted peri-mortem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about this later on. But now for another question. utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If not, why not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say 30 or 33?
