So not 27 cases but six cases. In the other cases, in 19 other cases -- well, I'll tell you something more about these cases with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In one case, the individual had a wire outside the body. That's number 2. Number 3, there were wire handcuffs on the joints. It doesn't say whether the hands were tied up or where the hands were. All it says is that there were wire handcuffs. And then wire handcuffs on the left and right wrist. So it doesn't say where the hands were. And this is why I'm saying why the reports are very superficial. You can't get a clear vision. Then it says wire ligatures on the hands attached in a bag, attached. Then it says, wire handcuffs on the left and right wrist. And then it says the same again. And then it says wire ligatures by the body. Then wire ligatures no specific location. It just says wire ligatures. It doesn't say whether they were taken off the hands or the legs or whether they were by the body and so on. Then it says wire ligatures around the hands, wire ligatures on the wrists. Shoe laces were used to attach the wrist. Then it says part of the wire outside of the bag for evidence. Then it says wire taken from the left wrist. Then it says wrist tied with a wire. There was wire around the wrist. And then wire ties. And then you can say -- see that it says something about the ligature being around the waist. I can't really understand this. Then wires around the left and right wrist. Wires taken off the left and right wrist. So I have now told you what it says for each autopsy report. So out of the 25 ligatures that were found, not 27 but 25, only six cases had their hands tied behind their backs. That's what it says in the autopsy reports. So this conclusion, Haglund's conclusion, is erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you're referring to this conclusion --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The one I read through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just conclude. Are you referring to the conclusion that all the victims had their hands tied behind their backs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: To that conclusion, too, and to the conclusion on the number of ligatures found at that site. Not 27 but 25, and also I have in mind the conclusion on their hands tied behind their backs, so both conclusions are not precise, not to say correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As an expert, what does it mean if the report says that the ligature was in a bag? Can you draw the conclusion that someone was tied up with that ligature from such a statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: This would mean that I would need other information to come to such a conclusion. The person who put that in the bag should have statement saying that it was taken off the body or found by the body, because when we were performing exhumations, when you come across a body, when you find a body, anything that is on the body, beneath the body or by the body, any evidence found is put in a certain bag so that it can subsequently be identified as, for example, something that was used to tie the witness up with. Glass can be found by the body, for example, that by a certain body. So I can't discuss whether this concerns a specific body or whether it's just something that was collected as evidence, evidence that was found by the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned certain deficiencies when it comes to the external findings. I'd like to ask you something else now. I noticed that in a certain number of autopsy reports, or rather in all of them, there were sketches of the corpses exhumed, and descriptions were given of the wounds, there were photographs that were also attached, so I wanted to ask you whether that fact might mean that the descriptions of the external and internal findings and of the trauma findings don't necessarily have to be complete because we have photographs too.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Both photos and sketches that may exist cannot replace or make up for the insufficient description. The description has to be complete because the sketches only document the description. Now, you can ask me why can't they replace them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. This is what I was going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It seems that I'm putting questions to myself because it only seemed logical that this calls for an explanation. If in a photo you see a damage like I've described it, a damage that has even been measured, that photo does not depict all the elements that I myself noticed during examination, and as I notice them, I have to describe them in the autopsy report so as to enable everybody who may read the report later how I had arrived at the conclusion. For example, there is a photo of damage to the skull, either regular circular or irregular circular defect, and to all of us this means this is a trauma to the head. However, the autopsy expert has to describe the edges and the sides of the defect, the angle at which they fall, because this is something that the photo cannot show. The contents on the edges, for example, if you put your hands like that, you can see this edge or the other edge, but the internal contents that reflect the mechanism that inflicted the wound, for example if it is a projectile, it leaves traces and you can prove that it was done by a projectile and so on and so forth, and because of that reason, during my autopsy I describe both the edges, the contents, the sides, I follow the channel, I describe the way the channel curves, whether it's straight or whether it's curvy. All these are elements pointing to evidence that will help me conclude about the mechanism of woundings, the type of projectile, whether it was blunt, whether it was sharp. This is the ABCs of our profession, and if that is missing, a mere photo cannot be evidence. It can only serve as something useful if it accompanies a complete description, and what we see here is incomplete descriptions. We see nothing but mere statements saying that this is it and you have to take it for the face value.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you tell me something else about your approach? Would that be a standard that is applied only in our parts, i.e. in Serbia, or is this a standard that would normally be applied all over the world?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that this is the standard of the profession all over the world, not only in our parts. And in order to confirm what I'm saying, I can give you an illustration. I've worked with an expert team from Finland who were working in Racak. They had their own team working for the Tribunal and they were dealing with the cases, the 40 of them, that were found in Racak. I don't know whether you remember Racak, which happened in 1999. I was one of the experts. There were four of us who were working together, and there were two experts from Russia, and we performed autopsies, we compiled autopsy reports and we applied a methodology which is customary and adopted all over the world starting with the external findings, taking photos and then a detailed description of what we observed. The Finnish experts did that, the report exists, we did that, so this is a customary standard. There may be slight differences in the words we use to describe things but what is described is well known. You have to describe the edges, the direction, the channel, the contents and all those things. The use of the words is not important. What needs to be described is what matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to move on to the other autopsy findings from Nova Kasaba. If I'm not mistaken we are talking about numbers 6, 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Since I cannot provide much comment here, it is my duty as a professional to say something before I answer your question. I would like to provide a comment, however, on the report, the same report by Mr. Haglund, in which he summarises all his pathological analysis and provides an example. NKS 1-6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I've already moved on to number 6, 7, 8. I will go back to the conclusions about the Nova Kasaba site 1, 2, 3 and 4. I'm now asking you about Nova Kasaba 6. I'm not asking you about the sixth grave from the first site.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. My answer about these particular sites, 6, 7 and 8, is that the descriptions of the wounds there are very correct, generally speaking, in a majority of the cases. There are minor objections, but I will accept that those were less experienced physicians who had used some previous reports and established their diagnosis based on that, but in general terms there is -- there are very correct descriptions of the mortal remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to go back to the conclusions. What you've been talking about and when you say that the descriptions are correct, do you mean to say that they were done according to the rules of the forensic profession?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: For the largest part, I have to say that these three sites have been described in much more precise terms than the previous sites. It is a fact, and it is very obvious when you look at those descriptions and reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I've interrupted you but I would like to ask you to go back to the conclusions that concern Nova Kasaba 1, 2, 3 and 4. First of all, tell me this: What are the conclusions based on according to the rules of profession? We are talking about autopsy reports and the conclusions thereof.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: A conclusion in an autopsy report has to represent an objective judgement of what has been established by the findings. In other words, a conclusion depends on the findings. If the findings change, the conclusion will have to change accordingly and vice versa. What I'm saying, a conclusion is an objective representation of what the findings, both external and internal findings, have established. Which means if there is a defect in the skull which has been described with all its characteristics and which points to the fact that the defect was inflicted by a projectile or a blunt object, then in the conclusion, this has to be stated to the same effect. In other words, the conclusion about the trauma examination has to be done in that way. When it comes to the conclusion about the cause of death, if that's what you are referring to, that conclusion, if the corpses are putrefied, it mustn't say that the cause of death is a gunshot wound because this cannot be proven by autopsy. You cannot prove that a gunshot wound was inflicted upon the corpse that is now putrefied. First you have to say that this is a corpse and then in the conclusion you have to state all the wounds that were inflicted upon that body. Once the Court collects all the other evidence and all the other elements within the context of the two facts that the body is putrefied and that there are gunshot wounds, it may conclude with more or less certainty that that was indeed the cause of death. In order for me to explain this, let me say what this means. The gunshot wound which cannot be proven that it cannot be said that it was inflicted during the life, it could have really been inflicted during the life but it could have also been inflicted post-mortem, because it would show the same characteristics in both cases, if the situation is examined on a putrefied body. What I'm saying is that I accept that this is a gunshot wound to the skull but I don't have any medical element to prove that that wound was inflicted during the life. And that's why I'm not allowed to conclude that this was indeed the cause of death because that same person, for example, if it was shot at while it was dying or after that, it could have also suffered from the gunshot wounds of the chest, which is soft tissue, without affecting any hard parts of the body. That person could have been poisoned. This person's throat might have been slit. In other words, wherever there is tissue which is now putrefied and where there could have been a wound which can now -- which cannot be proven, we only can prove one gunshot wound in the skull. That is why the cause of death is not something that you can state for a fact. You have to say this is a putrefied body and the autopsy only cannot establish the cause of death. However, the autopsy report in its conclusion has to state all the findings and there has to be a segregation between the mechanism of wound infliction. For example, a gunshot or a fracture of the arm that was inflicted by a blunt wound, so in the future when somebody collects some other evidence, a question will be raised and a question will be put to the expert, how do you know that it was a blunt wound, do you know if they were inflicted before the wound on the head or after the wound on the head? That's why you have to be very cautious when establishing the cause of death. And here it says that the cause of death is multiple gunshot wounds and this almost points to the fact that the doctor who performed the autopsy is absolutely sure that the wounds were inflicted before death, which points to another conclusion, and that is that all gunshot wounds are considered to be inflicted ante-mortem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Peri-mortem, in other words, which means immediately before death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say this has been agreed, what do you mean when you say this has been agreed, who has agreed upon that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me try and find this, and if need be we can display it on the screen. P575. I apologise, could you please repeat the number that you have just quoted from your document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: ERN 00912281-305. This is the document in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] It is P575, second page. [Interpretation] Do you see this on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Just a moment. Let me say that we need to go to the next paragraph, work in the morgue. You're looking at it now, a report on autopsies. This is all part of the standard. Whatever he has written, I can accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to my previous question. You said that you found something in Dr. Clark's report.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going back to that.

utterances.text: Go to the next page, please. This is it. Thank you. Scroll down a little, please. Move on, scroll down, please.

utterances.text: Do you want us to go to the next page?

utterances.text: Could you please scroll up a little? Very well. That's it. The second paragraph. No, no, no, no, no. That's it. [In English] Okay. Thank you. utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did but in order to arrive at that we have to say the following first. This was a real problem because the fracture which happens ante-mortem looks identical as the one inflicted post-mortem. This is what Mr. Clark states. I know it and I fully accept it. But after that, a reason is introduced when it is said this: "In all cases with certain exceptions it is considered that every wound which points to the damage --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This was too fast, the interpreter cannot interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, you're going too fast. I think you need to start again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to start again your answer to this question or repeat what you've said in any case. And slowly, please, so that the interpreters can catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you should quote starting with the sentence, "In all cases though there are certain exceptions." That's where you stopped.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I'll quote: "In all these cases" I have to read through the entire paragraph. I apologise. I'll read through the entire paragraph. So starting with the second paragraph: "This involved certain difficulties when it came to determining whether a certain wound had been caused before death or after death. That was a very real problem because a fracture that occurs ante-mortem, before death, is identical to a fracture that occurs post-mortem, after death, provided it has been caused in the same manner. Observing the damage to the soft tissue in the vicinity, for example, observing bruises or bleeding is the only way in which one can determine whether there is a difference. In the case of decomposed bodies, this becomes exceptionally difficult. And when only the skeletons remain, it's impossible. Therefore, strictly speaking, it will never be possible to state, for example, that a hole in the skull occurred before death and not after death. And this also concerns other types of wounds, or any other types of wounds in any other place on the body." So this is what I already told you. Now, let's move on. However, common sense should be used in this equation, and to suggest that these men died in some mysterious way and that they were then systematically shot at after they had died and that some of them were shot at several times, well, such an explanation is not credible. Therefore, in all of these cases, with certain exceptions, we are of the opinion that any injury that caused damage or indicated damage caused by a bullet, any such injury was caused while the individual was alive, and therefore it was necessarily or potentially fatal. So this is my answer. This is an assumption, that the wounds were inflicted by firearms while the individuals concerned were alive and therefore these wounds are the causes of death. These are the assumptions we are dealing with, assumptions that have been accepted or that are accepted by all pathologists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I may, Professor Dunjic, so that I try to understand better, if it had been you who were conducting these post-mortems and trying to prepare reports on each post-mortem, in the circumstances that are illustrated here, how would you have dealt with it? In other words, let me present to you a scenario. A scenario where you're told by investigators, we have information that several individuals were killed, shot, and then buried, from there even transported here or buried here and they have been exhumed now, and let's say that all these bodies are either completely decomposed, there is no soft tissue to let you establish whether the firearm wound is pre or post death or it's completely -- it's a complete skeleton so you can never really establish whether it was before or after, but you have this information and you find them with their hands tied and all other circumstances, how would you reach your conclusion as an experienced pathologist? In other words, would you have written the same things as we have and which you have just read out to us or would you have presented them differently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite frank, Your Honour, I must say that I've given much thought to this matter, as a professional, as someone who has been involved in this field for a long time. What I as an expert can tell this Tribunal concerns facts, transparent facts that can be verified. And this is regardless of investigators' reports. They compile their own reports. Anthropologists compile their own reports. Forensic experts such as myself draft their own reports, autopsy reports. My job is to present you with certain facts. You have previous information and so do I. People have been killed, firearms were used to kill people. But I have to tell you whether there are any firearm wounds, what kind of firearm wounds, I have to say where these people were hit, which parts of their bodies were hit, but when I provide you with this information I also have to demonstrate that this is the case. I have to do this by using a report, not photographs, and it's only then that these matters will have a certain validity. I can then draft a report and say that all the individuals I examined, five or ten individuals, at certain site, were in such and such a state of decomposition and I can then say that they died during the same period of time. That's one conclusion. The second conclusion would be that we assessed that this occurred at such and such a time. We will say that the period of time concerns the time from which they died until the time at which the autopsy was performed. I could say that certain individuals were hit by bullets, that they have wounds that are consistent with bullet wounds. You would ask me about the cases concerned and I would provide you with the relevant information but I don't have this information here in relation to Nova Kasaba. So the report does have to have or rather contain all those elements if it is to be a professional report. I cannot start assuming that they were alive, or rather they were in fact alive, but I cannot assume or speculate that they were shot at after death or before death, so there has to be other evidence from other witnesses, and so on the basis of that evidence that the Court should reach a conclusion. We performed autopsies in Batajnica. There were about 800 putrefied bodies. For all of them we stated that the following was the cause of death: I can just repeat this for you. Item 1, the corpse in an advanced state of decomposition, impossible to establish the cause of death. Then item 2, 3 or 4 of the conclusion we would give a detailed description of all the wounds observed. And then the Court must use other evidence, other testimony, in order to reach a conclusion. As a pathologist, I can understand the assumptions that have been written down here but I would have never have drafted such assumptions myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dunjic. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something else about this answer. When you draft your autopsy reports, when you give external findings, internal findings, trauma findings and when you give your conclusions which should be based on such analysis, when you do this, from the point of view of forensic medicine, can you use statements given by witnesses or investigators or by some of the parties, by the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused? Can you take such statements into consideration when you compile your autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: No, I can't. I am provided with information. For example I perform an autopsy. I'm ordered to perform an autopsy by an investigative court. I do the autopsy. I do this with the crime police. We state where the corpse was discovered, what was found by the corpse. This is the source of information for me. And this information should guide me. How should it guide me? Well in the following way. For example if it is said that the corpse was found in the street or rather in a forest, by a path, one needs to observe the characteristics of the corpse in detail. And then I can assess the age of the corpse, the time of death, and then I can move on. I can move on to internal and external findings, and then move on until I reach a conclusion about the cause of deaths. So this information is available. It's on the side. But when performing the autopsy, first there is a phase that precedes the autopsy and during that phase I receive information about the health condition of the deceased on whom I have to perform an autopsy or I receive such information subsequently. I receive such information from close relatives of the person concerned, for example. And I can only check up on this information when I compare this information to the findings. They might say that the man was ill and I don't come to such a conclusion. Such information provides me with certain guidelines. I pay attention to such information. But to be more specific with regard to how I proceeded, I have information obtained from witnesses and from you. I have familiarised myself with the case, I have information from witnesses, but I don't assess a witness's statement in the same way as the Court does, for example. Someone might tell me that someone was killed by firearms or that a burst of fire was directed at a person or that someone stood on a mine or some other explosive device was used to kill a person. This information is very important for me in the context of the findings that I will obtain in the course of the autopsy. So here, for example, I have five corpses, and these corpses don't seem to have been killed as a result of explosions but in other cases that's not the case. The autopsy provides indirect confirmation of such findings. But if this is to be useful to the Court, one has to have documents that provide valid descriptions of what actually occurred and then we can tie up the individual to the site, to the autopsy, and to witness statements. We can link all these elements but up but the witness statement cannot influence me, nor can the Prosecution statement influence me or evidence of any other kind. So this just represents other information that can serve as a guideline but the autopsy findings are of paramount importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else. In the case of Nova Kasaba 1, 2 and 3 and the one case that relates to the fourth grave site, did you find any inconsistencies between the conclusions and the findings, the external and internal findings and the trauma findings?

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, let us try to summarise the discussion about the mass grave 1/6. Could you please briefly tell us again what the inconsistencies are between the trauma report, the cause of death, the conclusion and the finding in the collective report?

utterances.text: The inconsistencies are obvious. If I may have a moment. It is the following: On one hand, we have post-mortem injuries without vital reactions with relatively precise descriptions; on the other hand, that the cause of death is unascertained precisely because of that. utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to move to some other inconsistencies, if any, in the conclusions concerning Nova Kasaba, the reports 1 and 2.

utterances.text: And 3.

utterances.text: In the trauma report, which is relatively precise, it says in item 1, Gunshot wound the diameter of which is 1 by 1 centimetre in the temporal occipital region. And internal cone-like damage on the left-hand side of the skull, partially going towards the left side of the back of the skull as well as to the left temple and the area of the maxilla. Item 2: Sequential fractures on the right collar bone and the second right rib from the back towards the front side, without a clearly pronounced cone-like damage that would correspond to a firearm wound. In items 2 and 3, we have a trauma finding which is not convincing in terms of proving that a projectile from a firearm caused the injuries. It exists as a possibility only. We do have the trauma, though. What is the inconsistency? Well, it's the cause of death, because it is stated there that there were multiple gunshot wounds, whereas we only have only one relatively precisely described wound in the area of the skull. That is the inconsistency. And I won't go into commenting the manner of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the cases in the Nova Kasaba 2 file, in several findings, I noticed the following, and the findings I refer to are 2/9, 12 and 13, and I'll have the precise e-court numbers after the question. I noticed that as the cause in the conclusion, it is stated that the injuries were caused by a high-velocity projectile. Let us please have a look at that finding. It is 2/9. In the B/C/S, it is page 191. In the English, it should be page 185.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: [In English] Scroll down, please. Next page. And next page. It's okay.

utterances.text: One moment. We are still waiting for the English page. This is the page. We can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: First, I have to read it out to see what the pathologist's description of the injury was. "A great damage of the skull including the left temporal bone, the left part of the frontal lobe, and the left part of the back of the skull, the left part of the mandibula, and break-up fractures corresponding to an injury caused by a firearm." In the conclusion it says, "The wound to the head caused by a firearm." When I say the conclusion, I mean the cause of death. From this description, save for the damage to the skull and the particular parts of the bones, I cannot conclude anything else. I cannot conclude, first of all, that this was caused by a firearm projectile. It is possible but the description is not there. Secondly, this type of injury was -- could have been caused by a blunt instrument of any sort or a large or small piece of shrapnel. And the third thing I cannot conclude is whether there were any vital reactions that may have been the cause of death, as I've explained previously. That is to say, the description of the injury provided, if compared to the relatively correct one from before, the NKS 1/6 case, it becomes clear to what extent this degree is insufficient. We have no description of the edges, sides or anything. Not even the lines of the fractures, which can only partially point to an explosive tool used, such as Mr. Haglund concluded when he talked about a small-calibre projectile of high velocity, if you recall that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that has to do with the next finding, which is 2/12. In the B/C/S it is page 202. Yes. And the English, it is 195. Could we please go to -- two pages after this one in the B/C/S. That is to say, page 204 in the B/C/S. This is 2-12. Yes, the trauma report. That's it.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The pathologist documents the trauma as follows: "Item 1 is extreme fracture of the skull with fragmentation." We have the middle bones of the face missing, save for one part of the maxilla. The cranial part is preserved. However, the entire left temporal area is missing as well as the back of the head. Item 2, the -- there is a fracture to the mandibula.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at the cause of death, which is the next page in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: [In English] No, no, no, no, scroll down, scroll down, next page, uh-huh. Yes. [Interpretation] The cause of death, a head injury caused by a projectile fired from a firearm at great speed. The manner of death, murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since it is said here that the head injury was caused by a projectile of high velocity, can you tell us, from the point of view of forensic medicine, with such a description of the trauma, can it be ascertained whether, indeed, there was a projectile of high velocity?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Based on the description provided that I read out, one cannot conclude anything except for the fact that there were defects to the skull and that some bones of the skull were missing, some parts of the skull. That is the only conclusion one can arrive at. As for the description itself, if I may have a moment, does not point to the fact that some of the -- that the injuries were caused by a projectile. There is no indication of it whatsoever. A projectile fired from a rifle, for example, moves at great speed. I believe it is around 800 metres per second. At the point of impact with the body, the speed is between 600 and 800 metres per second and it is a medium-high velocity. Once such a projectile pierces the skull, it creates a lot of damage. It's a fact. One can find traces on the bones of different shapes from the point of entry or exit of the projectile. However, the injuries of the skull, identical to the ones described here when we have parts of the skull missing, could also have been caused by a piece of shrapnel, that is to say pieces of an explosive device when hitting the skull. Such injuries could also have been caused by a blunt instrument. Also, when discussing low-velocity and low-calibre projectiles, even when fired point blank, create a lot of fractures, always leaving a trace. During putrefaction and decomposition, parts of the bones become separated, disarticulated, once the soft issue is gone. The longer the time, the more missing pieces of the skull we have, whereas originally these have been numerous fractures with many pieces of the skull. If I would receive such a skull I would never make the conclusion made here. It would have been but one of the possibilities indicating that it may have been a high-velocity projectile. It is only one possibility in speaking from the point of forensic medicine. The very description provided, with its characteristics, and with the things that should have been described, does not point to that particular thing. The only conclusion one can make is that we have the defects of the skull.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean to say that there are no indications which would prove that it was caused by a projectile?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC

utterances.text: This is a trauma that should have been inflicted ante-mortem, which means before death, when any sort of previous injury is mentioned. However, this description does not allow me to answer your question. And I can't tell you whether this trauma was caused before death and what is the basis of this statement, and as for the head trauma that I've quoted here, if we just remind ourselves what I read in the previous case, the description of the skull defect of certain dimensions with linear fractures, again I don't have here any other indicator pointing to the type of that trauma or that defect. [In English] Page down. Next page, next page, please. [Interpretation] As for the cause of death, it says, "Extreme head trauma. Extreme head trauma."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Now if you compare the description given in here, what we have here is the statement that there is a head trauma involved. And I'm not going to go into discussion on the cause of death. An identical description that we saw in the previous case of the similar skull defect speaks very precisely about a wound inflicted from a high-velocity firearm, so we have very similar descriptions and in one case --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Are you talking about a projectile that was a high-velocity projectile?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: This is a head wound inflicted by a projectile fired at a high velocity, and this is very similar to the description of this head trauma, and I apologise if I have confused the matters a little bit here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the injuries are described in a very similar way in the previous findings, and in this findings, but the causes differ?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are different. In the second case that I have quoted, which is the case that we have in front of us now, the last case, case 2/13, the only thing that is mentioned is trauma, which has not been defined, whether it was caused by a projectile, by a shrapnel, whether it is a wound inflicted by a blunt object before death or after death, and from their conclusion, one could deduct that it was inflicted before death, and I cannot accept that because there is no single piece of evidence proving that, but let me not repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like you to look at another findings, the following one. Page 201 in English. Page 201 in English, and in B/C/S it is page number 210. Again, you see the description of a skull trauma, 2/14, you see it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is again from Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: [In English] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] It is English page 202 and B/C/S page 211.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Next page?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Next page, in B/C/S. Yeah. That's it.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: That's okay. [Interpretation] Here we have proof of injury, which is the descriptive part of the trauma or the internal findings. Under 1, damage of the left temporal region, size 1 by 1.30 centimetres with a cone-like internal damage. Under 2, a fracture of the fourth right rib and the tip of the chest bone. Now, if I want to analyse this case very carefully, it says here that the cause of death is a skull trauma. The damage of the left temporal region is what it is, the size is 1 by 1.3. It points to a possible projectile wound because only a projectile causes a cone-like injury internally. As for the item 2, this is just a statement, no description of the external examination of the rib. So let's leave that aside. The cause of the head trauma, again, a general -- how shall I put it -- a general statement is taken into account and it is stated that the cause of death was the head injury. Here, the skull trauma has not been explained, i.e. no cause of trauma has been explained. It hasn't been stated whether it was caused by projectile, by shrapnel or a blunt object, because there is no other proof, no X-ray or anything, and the pathologist just concluded that it was a head trauma without any specifications. Therefore here we have a combination of a very generalised conclusion about the trauma and the relatively imprecise in one part and in another part a little bit more precise description of the trauma findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to move on to something else. You've told us that these findings, the autopsy findings, for the graves in Nova Kasaba number 6, 7 and 8 are rather correct and that they have been done according to the rules of the profession. In your findings, you have commented upon that. Before we move on to your report on these graves, could you please provide us with a general picture of these autopsy findings concerning Nova Kasaba? What can you tell bus the findings, the conclusions, the causes of death and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: There are two things here that I would like to highlight. First of all, Nova Kasaba number 6, 7 and 8, in the description of the main injuries, there is a very precise description of the injuries, which can help a professional in concluding that those indeed were injuries of certain kind. The descriptions of some bone fractures, not only of the skull but also of all the other bones is very precise, so one can easily draw conclusions based on that. For example, in one of the cases, Nova Kasaba 6, body number 1, there is a very precise description of the trauma, and I'm talking in very general terms about this trauma. Those were actually bone injuries. And the pathologist precisely describes all the elements that should be contained in a post-mortem report. However, when it comes to the cause of death, he had certain reservations, and irrespective of the very detailed description, he said that it was impossible to establish the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is Nova Kasaba 6 or --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Nova Kasaba 6, case number 1001. 001. Not 1001 but 001. I'm just correcting the transcript here. In the second case found at the same site, the head trauma has been described very well, in great detail and with a great precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just give me a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. We have been given a wrong report. Just ignore my question, and please describe the situation. We'll try and obtain the correct thing, Nova Kasaba 6.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In general terms, I have quoted something that I have put in my report in a very detailed form, and I can only say that the descriptions correspond to the diagnosis and this is what I can say in general terms about these three sites, Nova Kasaba 6, 7 and 8. Without offering any comments on the cause of death, but -- and I emphasise that -- but what is important and what differs, these three locations, sites, from the previous three sites is the very detailed descriptions of the findings, which indeed confirm that the injuries were inflicted with firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In general terms, can you now tell us something about the graves in Nova Kasaba under numbers 6, 7 and 8? Are they primary graves?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are primary graves according to the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you also tell us, in very general terms, what was the status of the bodies found in those graves? What was their condition?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Judging by the description of the external appearance of the mortal remains, there is a lack of precision in the description of the degree of putrefaction that I have already emphasised before. For example, in most of the cases, what is said is a complete body with clothes, but only the bones are present but no soft tissue. This is a rather correct description. But there are descriptions lacking detail on the degree of putrefaction and where those -- where the soft tissue is preserved, which does not help the forensic expert to conclude anything about the possible time of death. So these are the general shortcomings and deficiencies that I could easily apply to all the other sites that I had an opportunity to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the bodies, as far as I understood you, there was the presence of soft tissues at the moment of autopsy, at least in some of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: You're talking about mortal remains?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, mortal remains. Was there any difference noticed in the degree of what you call it, skeletonisation or putrefaction or the decomposition of those soft tissues in the bodies that were found in these particular graves?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: There is a difference in the description of the putrefaction and decomposition. Some bodies are completely skeletonised and some other sites there are soft tissues that were subject to putrefaction, to the degree of very deep saponification. Let me just quote NK 8. That's the site. And the case number is 46. It says here, "Soft tissues at head on the hands whereas the trunk is deeply saponified." What I'm reading here about the saponification, I as an expert can conclude that this part of the body had been exposed to high humidity, i.e. that it had been lying in a body of water or that there was water in the grave, or that it had previously lay in some humid conditions that had created conditions for the onset of saponfication, and based on such description, one can assume or conclude whether the body was in humid conditions before the burial or in the grave itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you this as well as some other findings tomorrow, but before that, let me ask you to explain this term saponification because this is as very technical term that we have not come across before.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: This is a degree of putrefaction. This is a specific type of changes on the soft tissue which is of some importance for -- to us forensic experts. Where there is saponification, that means that that part of the body or the whole body lay in high humidity, and those soft tissues transformed into soap. Later on, on a body saponified in this way, calcium is deposited on that part of the body, and the -- this turns into a saponified remains. This is very important for establishing the time of death, the time of death from the time of death to the moment of saponification. And at the same time, a body saponified in this way or putrefied in this way allow the pathologist to notice even those changes, for example wounds or injuries, which he could not have noticed in the initial stages of putrefaction. So when you say saponification, you mean the degree of putrefaction in which the tissue is so much altered that it looks like soap or can be calcified, and this is why it is very important to describe in very tiny detail which parts of the body have been saponified, which have been skeletonised and the latter term implies a complete lack of soft tissues and the fact that the bones are completely bare. There's are the same thing as in the disarticulation of joints which happens due to putrefaction and is also used to establish the time of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we can leave it at that. We will continue tomorrow, Professor Dunjic, and I wish you all a very nice evening. Thank you.
